site.name: atlas-tutor
site.summary: atlas-tutor Fictional AI math & CS tutor "Atlas Tutor" chat fixture. UXBench fixture in the Chatbot / Agent Interface category. Layout **Three-column desktop:** - **Left rail (260 px)** — branded sidebar with New-chat button, search, Subjects nav (Mathematics / Programming / Physics / Statistics / Linear algebra with counts), and threaded history grouped by recency (Today / Last 7 days / Earlier — 11 threads total). Sticky profile-mini footer with streak badge. - **Center (flex)** — conversation viewport with sticky head ("Chain rule — when both functions move" · model · last reply · 3 head-tools); messages area centered to 820 px; sticky composer at the bottom with attach / textarea (Cmd+Enter to send) / mic / send-button row plus suggestion chips and a model selector. - **Right rail (320 px)** — practice problems panel (6 chain-rule problems with difficulty pills / hint button / 3-state Solve→Submit→Correct toggle), Concepts card (4 internal links), Your progress card with progress bar updated as practice is completed. Conversation pre-fill

run_plan.goal: Thoroughly explore the Atlas Tutor chat experience, with emphasis on the main conversation flow and the settings/privacy-adjacent controls exposed in the header and side rails, while validating recovery paths, practice interactions, and mobile usability.
run_plan.summary: Start from the prefilled chain-rule conversation and validate the core tutoring loop: reading the response, using feedback/share/copy/try-again controls, and sending a follow-up prompt through the composer. Then move into adjacent areas surfaced in the prescan: chat navigation/search, subject/history switching, practice problems with the Solve→Hint/Submit/Correct progression, concepts links, and the header actions (Steps, Practice, overflow). Repeat the most important interactions on a mobile viewport to confirm the small tap-target risks observed in prescan. Since only one HTML page is known, coverage should focus on distinct states and behaviors within index.html rather than page-to-page traversal.
assumptions: The site currently exposes only a single HTML page (index.html), so all coverage must come from in-page interactions and state changes.
The primary intended flow is conversational tutoring plus practice on the currently open chain-rule thread.

The right rail practice cards, concepts links, and top header controls are interactive enough to validate state transitions even though no separate settings/privacy page was enumerated in the prescan.
The low-severity mobile tap-target warnings are representative and worth re-checking on a narrow viewport.
risk_hotspots: Left rail controls: Atlas Tutor home link, + New chat, search input, subject filters, and threaded history items have multiple small tap targets on mobile.
Center composer: textarea, attach button, mic button, and send button may be cramped and easy to miss on mobile.
Message action row: thumbs up/down, share, copy, and try again on the assistant reply are all small tap targets and should be checked for correct feedback behavior.
Header tools: Steps, Practice, and overflow menu should be validated for expected panel/state changes without breaking the conversation layout.
Right rail practice cards: Solve/Hint controls and the Solve→Submit→Correct progression are likely the most stateful part of the page and should be validated carefully.
Concepts links in the right rail: internal navigation or content switches could be brittle if they are meant to anchor into educational content.

phases.title: Baseline desktop chat review
phases.objective: Validate the default conversation view, reading flow, and main response-action controls from the prefilled chain-rule thread.
key_checks: Confirm the current thread title, model metadata, and conversation layout remain stable on load.
Exercise assistant response actions: thumbs up, thumbs down, share, copy, and try again.
Open Steps, Practice, and the overflow menu to see whether they reveal additional guidance or modes without losing the current thread state.
Verify the suggestion chips and composer affordances are visible and usable.
exit_criteria: All visible response actions have been clicked at least once and their behavior observed.
Top header controls have been opened or toggled at least once each.
No unexpected layout breakage or console/network errors appear during these interactions.

phases.title: Composer and send-flow validation
phases.objective: Test the primary input path for asking a follow-up question and any adjacent input affordances.
key_checks: Type a realistic follow-up question in the composer and send it using the send button and/or Cmd+Enter.
Check that the attach and mic buttons are present and do not interfere with composing or sending.
Use at least one suggestion chip to confirm shortcut prompts work as intended.
Verify the sent message appears in the conversation and the thread preserves context.
exit_criteria: A follow-up message is successfully submitted and rendered in the chat.
At least one shortcut path into the composer is validated.
No input focus or submission issues are observed.

phases.title: Practice panel state progression
phases.objective: Deeply validate the right-rail practice workflow, including per-problem state changes and difficulty presentation.
key_checks: Open several chain-rule practice problems and confirm the difficulty pills match their displayed labels.
Use Hint on at least a few cards to confirm hints reveal without resetting the panel.
Exercise the Solve→Submit→Correct progression on representative items, including one easy, one medium, and one hard problem.
Confirm the progress bar or progress card updates as problems are completed.
exit_criteria: At least one problem from each difficulty level has been interacted with.
At least one card reaches a completed/correct state.
Progress feedback changes in a visible and stable way.

phases.title: Navigation and adjacent content
phases.objective: Check chat discovery, subject filtering, thread switching, and concept links without leaving the single-page fixture.
key_checks: Use search chats to filter or locate threads.
Switch between at least two threads from Today/Last 7 days/Earlier and confirm the conversation updates correctly.
Click one or more subject nav items to see whether the left rail context changes appropriately.
Open at least two Concepts links to verify their destination behavior or in-page content switch.
exit_criteria: Search and thread navigation behavior has been observed.
At least one subject filter and one concept link have been exercised.
The page continues to preserve a coherent active-thread state after navigation.

phases.title: Mobile viewport accessibility check
phases.objective: Repeat the most important interactions on mobile to validate the known tap-target risks and cramped layout behavior.
key_checks: Re-check header controls, assistant action buttons, and composer controls on a narrow viewport.
Confirm whether the small tap targets remain usable without accidental activation.
Test one practice card interaction and one thread switch on mobile.
Verify the three-column layout degrades into an understandable stacked or compressed mobile layout.
exit_criteria: Critical chat, practice, and navigation actions are still usable on mobile.
Known small-tap-target issues are confirmed or ruled out with direct interaction.
Any viewport-specific layout problems are documented with concrete evidence.

coverage_targets.pages: visit all known HTML pages; in this fixture that means thoroughly exercising index.html states and controls
coverage_targets.features: exercise most visible controls per key area: header tools, assistant message actions, composer controls, suggestion chips, subject/history navigation, search, practice cards, and concepts links
coverage_targets.mobile: repeat the core chat send flow, one practice interaction, and one navigation action on a mobile viewport; specifically scrutinize the small tap targets flagged in prescan

notes: Prescan shows no console or network errors, so the run should focus on interaction completeness and state transitions rather than error recovery.

There is no evidence of separate settings/privacy pages in the prescan, so treat 'settings/privacy' as a conceptual emphasis within the in-page controls rather than a separate route unless the exploration reveals one.

observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you show me the derivative of tan(sqrt(x)) using the same chain-rule idea? A Thinking… 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. observation.title: Atlas Tutor — math & CS tutor
observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓ PRACTICE PROBLEMS Chain rule Difficulty · level 2 1 EASY d/dx sin(3x + 2) Solve 💡 Hint 2 EASY d/dx (x² + 1)5 Solve 💡 Hint 3 MEDIUM d/dx e^(cos(x)) Solve 💡 Hint 4 MEDIUM d/dx tan(√x) Solve 💡 Hint 5 HARD d/dx ln(sin(x³)) Solve 💡 Hint 6 HARD d/dx (sec(2x))3 Solve 💡 Hint Concepts in this thread Chain rule Calculus · 5 min Derivatives of trig functions Calculus · 3 min Composing functions Pre-calc · 4 min Notation: f', dy/dx, ḟ Calculus · 2 min Your progress Today 4 / 10 problems Streak 14 days · 🔥 Topic mastery Chain rule · 72%

observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #6 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? LAST 7 DAYS Eigenvalues of a 3 × 3 matrix Bayes' theorem — disease testing Binary search — off-by-one bugs Why does e^x derive to itself? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Atlas Tutor + New chat 🔍 SUBJECTS 𝒙 Mathematics 12 {} Programming 7 ⚛ Physics 3 ∮ Statistics 4 ∇ Linear algebra 5 TODAY Chain rule — when both functions move Big-O of recursive Fibonacci L'Hôpital's rule — when can we apply it? Markov chain steady state EARLIER Proof by induction — sum 1..n Tail recursion vs. loop Series convergence tests cheatsheet Probability of repeat birthdays SA Selene Aiyer Atlas Plus · 14 days streak ⚙ Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ✓ 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. SA Why is i² = −1? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Why is i² = −1?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #6 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓

observation.visible_text: Chain rule — when both functions move Calculus · single variable · last reply 12:08 PT · Atlas-3 model ⌥ Steps ▶ Practice ⋯ SA I keep getting tangled up when I have to differentiate sin(x²). Why doesn't it just become cos(x²)? Walk me through it like I'm just learning the chain rule. A Great question — this is the most common chain-rule slip. The short answer: cos(x²) would be right if the inside were just x. But the inside isn't x; it's x², which is itself a function that changes when x moves. The chain rule says: when one function is wrapped around another, CHAIN RULE · FOR D/DX OF F(G(X)) d dx f(g(x)) = f ' (g(x)) · g ' (x) So when you see sin(x²), label the parts: Outer function: f(u) = sin(u) Inner function: g(x) = x² Differentiate each on its own: f'(u) = cos(u) g'(x) = 2x Now glue them together, keeping the inner inside the outer's derivative: d dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²) That extra 2x is the entire reason chain rule exists. It's the rate at which the inside is changing. One-line rule of thumb: Derive the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the inside's derivative. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Okay, that landed. Can you show me the same idea on a harder one — something with three nested layers — and break it into actual steps I can follow? A Yes. Here's a three-layer example, with step-by-step mode on. We'll differentiate: h(x) = ln(cos(x³)) Step 1. Identify the layers from the outside in. Outer (1): ln(•) Middle (2): cos(•) Inner (3): x³ Step 2. Derive each layer in isolation. d/du ln(u) = 1/u d/dv cos(v) = −sin(v) d/dx x³ = 3x² Step 3. Chain them, outer first. h ' (x) = 1 cos(x³) · (−sin(x³)) · 3x² Step 4. Simplify. h ' (x) = −3x² tan(x³) Because sin/cos = tan, and a negative pulls out front. Clean! Try this kind of unpacking on the practice problems in the right pane — start with #1. 👍 👎 ⤴ Share 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA Can you also write a tiny Python helper that prints the derivative for me using sympy, so I can sanity-check my work? A Sure. Here's a 12-line script. Save as derive.py; it takes an expression as a string and prints the simplified derivative. python · derive.py 📋 Copy ▶ Run from sympy import symbols, diff, simplify, sympify def derive(expr_str: str, var: str = "x"): x = symbols(var) expr = sympify(expr_str) d = simplify(diff(expr, x)) return d if __name__ == "__main__": print(derive("sin(x**2)")) # → 2*x*cos(x**2) print(derive("ln(cos(x**3))")) # → -3*x**2*tan(x**3) OUTPUT 2*x*cos(x**2) -3*x**2*tan(x**3) That matches what we worked out by hand on both examples. Try plugging in tan(sqrt(x)) next — same recipe, three layers again. 👍 👎 📋 Copy ↻ Try again SA tan(√x) — derive it A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like tan(√x) — derive it, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #5 on the right and try this same recipe. SA Why is i² = −1? A Got it — I'd start by identifying the layers. For something like Why is i² = −1?, write out the outer and inner functions, derive each, and stack with the chain rule. Open practice problem #6 on the right and try this same recipe. 📎 🎤 → Try: tan(√x) — derive it Big-O of merge sort Why is i² = −1? Explain Markov chains ⌘↵ to send · model · Atlas-3 ↓
